Quadratic inequalities between the largest eigenvalues of a graphThanks: The author was supported by the Dynasnet ERC Synergy project (ERC-2018-SYG 810115) and the Hungarian National Research, Development and Innovation Office (Advanced grant 15337)

Roland Paulin Address: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics, H-1053 Budapest, Reáltanoda utca 13-15 Email address: paulinroland@gmail.com
Date: September 29, 2026
Abstract.

We prove a sharp quadratic inequality between the largest two eigenvalues λ1≥λ2\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2} of a graph with nn vertices. We also prove a quadratic inequality between the second and third largest eigenvalues λ2≥λ3\lambda_{2}\geq\lambda_{3}. These results in particular imply the bounds λ1+λ2≤87​n−2\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\leq\frac{8}{7}n-2, λ3≤n3−1\lambda_{3}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1 and λ2+λ3≤23​n−2\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}\leq\frac{2}{3}n-2. In fact we determine the closure of the set of possible (λ1+1n,λ2+1n)∈ℝ2(\frac{\lambda_{1}+1}{n},\frac{\lambda_{2}+1}{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and (λ2+1n,λ3+1n)∈ℝ2(\frac{\lambda_{2}+1}{n},\frac{\lambda_{3}+1}{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. More generally, we prove quadratic bounds in the case of symmetric matrices in [0,1]n×n[0,1]^{n\times n}, and we also give a quadratic bound for two eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix in [−1,1]n×n[-1,1]^{n\times n}. These bounds are proved by transforming the problem into extremal geometric questions in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. We use the method of Lagrange multipliers to reduce to special cases with at most five points, and we deal with these special cases directly.

Key words and phrases: 
graph eigenvalues, matrix eigenvalues

05C35, 05C50, 15A18, 15A42

1. Introduction

In this article we study the first, second and third largest eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix AGA_{G} of a graph GG, and more generally, of a symmetric matrix A∈[0,1]n×nA\in[0,1]^{n\times n}. Let λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\dotsc\geq\lambda_{n} be the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix AGA_{G}, where GG is a finite, simple graph with n≥2n\geq 2 vertices, and let si=λi+1ns_{i}=\frac{\lambda_{i}+1}{n}. It is known that s1≤1s_{1}\leq 1 and 0≤s2≤120\leq s_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2} (see [3]), and recently s3≤13s_{3}\leq\frac{1}{3} has been proved by Tang [8] (also see [7]), solving a problem of Nikiforov [6]. Recently Kumar, Liu, Monterde, Pragada and Tait [5] proved λ1+λ2≤87​n\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\leq\frac{8}{7}n, solving a conjecture of Ebrahimi B, Mohar, Nikiforov and Ahmady [1], and Huang and Wei [4] improved this to s1+s2≤87s_{1}+s_{2}\leq\frac{8}{7}.

We study the possible values of (s1,s2)∈ℝ2(s_{1},s_{2})\in\R^{2} and (s2,s3)∈ℝ2(s_{2},s_{3})\in\R^{2}. We prove that s12+s1​s2+2​s22≤s1+s2s_{1}^{2}+s_{1}s_{2}+2s_{2}^{2}\leq s_{1}+s_{2} and 2​(s22+s2​s3+s32)≤s2+s32(s_{2}^{2}+s_{2}s_{3}+s_{3}^{2})\leq s_{2}+s_{3}, and we prove that these bounds are sharp in a sense (Corollary 2.1). As a consequence we get s1+s2≤87s_{1}+s_{2}\leq\frac{8}{7}, s2+s3≤23s_{2}+s_{3}\leq\frac{2}{3} and s3≤13s_{3}\leq\frac{1}{3}. We prove quadratic inequalities not just for graphs, but more generally, for symmetric matrices A∈[0,1]n×nA\in[0,1]^{n\times n} (Theorem 2.1). We also prove a quadratic bound for two eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix B∈[−1,1]n×nB\in[-1,1]^{n\times n} (Theorem 2.2). We prove these results as a consequence of extremal geometric statements in ℝ3\R^{3} and in ℝ2\R^{2} (Propositions 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4). In the last extremal geometric problem (in the proof of Proposition 2.4), we use the method of Lagrange multipliers, and reduce the problem to the case of at most 55 points (with further restrictions as well), and we deal with these special cases directly.

We use the notation [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dotsc,n\} for n∈ℤ≥0n\in\Z_{\geq 0}. For symmetric square matrices A⪰BA\succeq B means A−BA-B is positive semidefinite, and A≻BA\succ B means A−BA-B is positive definite. If GG is a finite simple graph with vertex set [n][n], then AGA_{G} denotes its adjacency matrix. The characteristic polynomial of a matrix M∈ℝn×nM\in\R^{n\times n} is χM​(t)=det(t​In−M)\chi_{M}(t)=\det(tI_{n}-M). Let ℛ1,2\mcalR_{1,2} denote the set of (s1,s2)∈ℝ2(s_{1},s_{2})\in\R^{2} such that there is a sequence (Gi)i≥1(G_{i})_{i\geq 1} of finite, simple graphs, where GiG_{i} has nin_{i} vertices and eigenvalues λi,1≥…≥λi,ni\lambda_{i,1}\geq\dotsc\geq\lambda_{i,n_{i}}, and ni→∞n_{i}\to\infty and λi,a+1ni→sa\frac{\lambda_{i,a}+1}{n_{i}}\to s_{a} as i→∞i\to\infty for a∈{1,2}a\in\{1,2\}. Similarly, let ℛ2,3\mcalR_{2,3} denote the set of (s2,s3)∈ℝ2(s_{2},s_{3})\in\R^{2} such that there is a sequence (Gi)i≥1(G_{i})_{i\geq 1} of finite, simple graphs, where GiG_{i} has nin_{i} vertices and eigenvalues λi,1≥…≥λi,ni\lambda_{i,1}\geq\dotsc\geq\lambda_{i,n_{i}}, and ni→∞n_{i}\to\infty and λi,a+1ni→sa\frac{\lambda_{i,a}+1}{n_{i}}\to s_{a} as i→∞i\to\infty for a∈{2,3}a\in\{2,3\}. Let 𝒮1,2\mcalS_{1,2} and 𝒮2,3\mcalS_{2,3} be slight modifications of ℛ1,2\mcalR_{1,2} and ℛ2,3\mcalR_{2,3}, where we do not require ni→∞n_{i}\to\infty in the definition. So 𝒮1,2\mcalS_{1,2} is the closure of the set {(λ1​(G)+1|V⁡(G)|,λ2​(G)+1|V⁡(G)|);|V⁡(G)|≥2}⊆ℝ2\{(\frac{\lambda_{1}(G)+1}{|V(G)|},\frac{\lambda_{2}(G)+1}{|V(G)|});\,|V(G)|\geq 2\}\subseteq\R^{2} and 𝒮2,3\mcalS_{2,3} is the closure of the set {(λ2​(G)+1|V⁡(G)|,λ3​(G)+1|V⁡(G)|);|V⁡(G)|≥3}⊆ℝ2\{(\frac{\lambda_{2}(G)+1}{|V(G)|},\frac{\lambda_{3}(G)+1}{|V(G)|});\,|V(G)|\geq 3\}\subseteq\R^{2}. Clearly ℛ1,2⊆𝒮1,2\mcalR_{1,2}\subseteq\mcalS_{1,2} and ℛ2,3⊆𝒮2,3\mcalR_{2,3}\subseteq\mcalS_{2,3}. In Corollary 2.1 we give exact descriptions for ℛ1,2\mcalR_{1,2}, ℛ2,3\mcalR_{2,3}, 𝒮1,2\mcalS_{1,2}, 𝒮2,3\mcalS_{2,3}.

2. Statement of the results

The following theorem gives a quadratic inequality between the first and second largest eigenvalues, and an inequality between the second and third largest eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix in [0,1]n×n[0,1]^{n\times n}.

Theorem 2.1.

Let n≥2n\geq 2, and let A∈[0,1]n×nA\in[0,1]^{n\times n} be a symmetric matrix with eigenvalues λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\dotsc\geq\lambda_{n}. Let si=λins_{i}=\frac{\lambda_{i}}{n}. Then s1∈[0,1]s_{1}\in[0,1] and s2≤12s_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}. If s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0, then

(1) s12+s1​s2+2​s22≤s1+s2.s_{1}^{2}+s_{1}s_{2}+2s_{2}^{2}\leq s_{1}+s_{2}.

If n≥3n\geq 3 and s3≥0s_{3}\geq 0, then

(2) 2​(s22+s2​s3+s32)≤s2+s3.2(s_{2}^{2}+s_{2}s_{3}+s_{3}^{2})\leq s_{2}+s_{3}.
Remark 2.1.

The construction in the proof of Corollary 2.1 shows that the bounds here are sharp in some sense (assuming s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0 in the first inequality, and s3≥0s_{3}\geq 0 in the second one). The inequality s12+s1​s2+2​s22≤s1+s2s_{1}^{2}+s_{1}s_{2}+2s_{2}^{2}\leq s_{1}+s_{2} can fail if s2<0s_{2}<0, e.g., for A=(0110)A=(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{smallmatrix}) we get (s1,s2)=(12,−12)(s_{1},s_{2})=(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}). The inequality 2​(s22+s2​s3+s32)≤s2+s32(s_{2}^{2}+s_{2}s_{3}+s_{3}^{2})\leq s_{2}+s_{3} can fail if s3<0s_{3}<0, e.g., for A=(010101010)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&0&1\\ 0&1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right) we get (s1,s2,s3)=(23,0,−23)(s_{1},s_{2},s_{3})=(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},0,-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}).

Figures 1 and 2 show the regions of (s1,s2)(s_{1},s_{2}) and (s2,s3)(s_{2},s_{3}) defined by the above quadratic inequalities, with the requirements s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0 and s3≥0s_{3}\geq 0. As a consequence we get that s1+s2≤87s_{1}+s_{2}\leq\frac{8}{7}, and s2+s3≤23s_{2}+s_{3}\leq\frac{2}{3} and s3≤13s_{3}\leq\frac{1}{3} for n≥3n\geq 3. The condition s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0 is automatically satisfied if Ai,i=1A_{i,i}=1 for every i∈[n]i\in[n] (e.g., if A=In+AGA=I_{n}+A_{G} for a finite simple graph GG), because then 1=1n​Trace⁡(A)=∑i=1nsi≤s1+(n−1)​s21=\frac{1}{n}\Trace(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}\leq s_{1}+(n-1)s_{2} and s1≤1s_{1}\leq 1.

s12+s1​s2+2​s22≤s1+s2,s_{1}^{2}+s_{1}s_{2}+2s_{2}^{2}\leq s_{1}+s_{2},

and if n≥3n\geq 3, then

2​(s22+s2​s3+s32)≤s2+s3.2(s_{2}^{2}+s_{2}s_{3}+s_{3}^{2})\leq s_{2}+s_{3}.

If n≥3n\geq 3 and GG is not the path graph with 33 vertices, then s3≥0s_{3}\geq 0. The quadratic inequalities are sharp in the following sense:

𝒮1,2=ℛ1,2\displaystyle\mcalS_{1,2}=\mcalR_{1,2} ={(s1,s2)∈ℝ2; 0≤s2≤s1 and s12+s1s2+2s22≤s1+s2},\displaystyle=\{(s_{1},s_{2})\in\R^{2};\,0\leq s_{2}\leq s_{1}\textrm{ and }s_{1}^{2}+s_{1}s_{2}+2s_{2}^{2}\leq s_{1}+s_{2}\},
ℛ2,3\displaystyle\mcalR_{2,3} ={(s2,s3)∈ℝ2; 0≤s3≤s2 and 2(s22+s2s3+s32)≤s2+s3}\displaystyle=\{(s_{2},s_{3})\in\R^{2};\,0\leq s_{3}\leq s_{2}\textrm{ and }2(s_{2}^{2}+s_{2}s_{3}+s_{3}^{2})\leq s_{2}+s_{3}\}

and

𝒮2,3=ℛ2,3∪{(13,1−23)}.\mcalS_{2,3}=\mcalR_{2,3}\cup\left\{\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\right\}.

Proof of Theorem 2.1 ⇒\Rightarrow Corollary 2.1.

We apply Theorem 2.1 for the matrix A=In+AG∈[0,1]n×nA=I_{n}+A_{G}\in[0,1]^{n\times n} with eigenvalues λ1+1≥…≥λn+1\lambda_{1}+1\geq\dotsc\geq\lambda_{n}+1. If GG is the three-vertex path graph, then (s2,s3)=(13,1−23)(s_{2},s_{3})=(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{3}), and the quadratic inequality for s2,s3s_{2},s_{3} holds. Now we prove that if n≥3n\geq 3 and GG is not the three-vertex path graph, then λ3≥−1\lambda_{3}\geq-1 (and thus s3≥0s_{3}\geq 0). The Cauchy interlacing theorem implies that if HH is an induced subgraph of GG with at least 33 vertices, then λ3​(H)≤λ3​(G)\lambda_{3}(H)\leq\lambda_{3}(G). But the only 33 vertex graph HH with λ3​(H)<−1\lambda_{3}(H)<-1 is the path graph. So if λ3<−1\lambda_{3}<-1, then every three vertex induced subgraph of GG has exactly two edges. We also get ℛ1,2,ℛ2,3⊆ℝ≥02\mcalR_{1,2},\mcalR_{2,3}\subseteq\R_{\geq 0}^{2}, because in the definition of ℛ2,3\mcalR_{2,3} we require ni→∞n_{i}\to\infty as i→∞i\to\infty. Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
